title: Why I Started This Blog
summary: Some thoughts on why a personal, hand-rolled static site beats another profile on someone else's platform.
body:
I've started and abandoned a handful of "I'm going to write more" projects over the years — a Medium account, a Notion page I made public once, a half-finished newsletter. They all fizzled out for the same reason: I never felt like I actually *owned* the thing.

## What I wanted instead

A few requirements I kept coming back to:

- **No platform risk.** If a company shuts down or changes its terms, my writing shouldn't disappear with it.
- **No tracking I didn't choose.** Most blogging platforms ship analytics and ad scripts I never asked for.
- **Fast, boring, and durable.** Plain HTML loads instantly and will still work in ten years.

So I built exactly that: articles as JSON files in a git repo, a small Node script that renders them to static HTML, and [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com/) for hosting. No server, no database, no login page for strangers to poke at.

## The trade-off

It's slower to publish than typing into a text box on someone else's site — I have to run a local tool, review a diff, and push a commit. Honestly, that friction is a feature. It means everything that ends up live here is something I actually meant to publish.

More posts soon.
author: Charlie Cunningham
